title: Release Orchestration Across Many Services
summary: Coordinating deploys once you have more than a handful of independently-deployed services, so N pipelines still add up to one coherent release.

slides.markdown:
A single service with its own pipeline is simple: deploy it, watch it, done. The problem shows up at N services — each independently deployable — when a feature spans several of them. Deploying each service "whenever its pipeline finishes," with no coordination, risks a window where service A expects a contract service B hasn't shipped yet, producing errors no single service's own tests would catch.

Release orchestration is the layer above individual pipelines that manages this: sequencing changes across services so the system stays consistent mid-rollout, not just at the end.

Some changes have a hard order requirement: a database schema migration adding a column must land **before** the service reading that column deploys, or every request in between fails. The reverse is true for removing a column — the code that stops reading it must ship *before* the migration that drops it.

Orchestration means encoding this ordering explicitly (a migration step gated ahead of a deploy step, or a multi-service release pipeline with dependency edges) rather than trusting that everyone remembers the right sequence during a busy release.

The single most powerful tool for de-risking multi-service releases is **decoupling deploy from release**: ship the new code to all services behind a feature flag that's off, so the deploy itself carries almost no behavioral risk, then flip the flag on separately once every dependency is confirmed live.

This breaks the "everything must land in the same instant" pressure entirely — deploys can happen at whatever pace each service's pipeline runs, and the actual user-facing change activates only when you choose, independent of deploy timing.

Even with ordering and flags handled, a multi-service change is safer rolled out in **stages** rather than to 100% of traffic/tenants/regions at once — by percentage of traffic, by region, or by tenant. A staged rollout means a bad interaction between services is caught while it's affecting 1% of traffic or one region, not everyone simultaneously.

This is the same principle as a single-service canary (from the deployment-strategies-automation Topic), just applied across the coordinated set of services releasing together.

slides.sectionTitle: A backwards-incompatible change, rolled out safely
slides.markdown:
Worked example: an API's request field is renamed, and three downstream services call it. The safe sequence is: (1) the API adds the *new* field name while still accepting the old one (backwards-compatible dual-write), (2) each downstream service migrates to the new field name on its own pipeline's schedule, behind a flag if needed, (3) once all three confirm they've switched, the API removes support for the old field name.

At no point is there a single moment where every service must deploy simultaneously — the compatibility window is what buys the coordination slack.

The failure mode this whole discipline exists to prevent: a "release" defined as triggering every service's pipeline at the same time and hoping the ordering works out. Any dependency mistake — the wrong order, a service that's slower to deploy than expected — cascades into a multi-service outage that's far harder to diagnose than a single bad deploy, because the failure surface spans services with different owners and different logs.

The fix is everything in this Topic: explicit ordering, flags to decouple deploy from release, and staged rollout — never "deploy all N and see."
